Description: The source of this e-text is *Calcutta Sanskrit Series* 3—*Kaulajñānanirṇaya* and some minor texts of the school of Matsyendranātha—where it is bundled together with the *Kaulajñānanirṇaya*, the *Kulānandatantra*, and the *Jñānakārikā*.
The printed volume also contains introductory material and summaries in English.

The guru, the guru’s son, and others who are the guru’s kinsmen.
And among the others in order of seniority, I bow my head at their feet. || 1 ||
I bow down to that Guru who has transcended all mental cultivation;
the world wanders in delusion, while he, free from delusion, has reached firm certainty. || 2 ||
Those men established in the Primordial Lord attain success;
they are endowed with noble lineage and birth, and possessed of the virtues of excellent conduct. || 3 ||

"One who is endowed with devotion to the guru and possessed of wisdom is called a disciple," so it was said by Ādinātha, the one dwelling on the peak of Mount Kejāpūpa, when he was overcome with agitation. || 4 ||
Out of compassion alone, Mīnanātha also [taught] the supreme reality through awakening;
thus, Mīnanātha, being composed, replied to his excellent disciple.
"You are both teacher and disciple, and likewise disciple and teacher; O auspicious lady, between these two here, no equal attainment arises."
I am Mīnanātha, the lord of sages and son of Umā and Śaṅkara;
I shall proclaim the supreme reality that awakens one to both the Kula and Akula paths.
The Ādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddhi, and Ājñā—these are the six auspicious Kaula cakras. || 8 ||
The Ādhāra resides in the anus, and the Svādhiṣṭhāna is in the genitals;
Maṇipūra is located at the navel, and Anāhata is in the heart.
Purity is in the region of the throat, and the wheel of command (ājñācakra) is at the face between the eyebrows.
Having understood this as the piercing of the wheels, one reaches that which transcends the wheels, the stainless (nirañjana).
The *iḍā* flows in the left, and the *piṅgalā* flows in the right;
between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* is the *suṣumnā*, whose nature is bliss. || 11 ||
In the support (ādhāra), the genitals, the navel, the heart-lotus, the root of the palate, and the forehead;
in the two-petaled, sixteen-spoked, twenty-two-petaled, ten-petaled, twelve-petaled, six-petaled, and four-petaled [cakras];
at the tip of the nose, in the middle of the eyebrows, and in the region of the throat accompanied by the letters ḍa, pha, ka, tha, and sa, as well as the vowels.
I bow to the form of the letters situated on all the petals, which is endowed with the meaning of reality: Haṃ Kṣaṃ. || 12 ||
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—these, joined with the five organs of action, are endowed with the power of activity. || 13 ||
Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya are endowed with the five organs of perception and possessed of the power of intellect. || 14 ||
The fire is situated in the center of the *śakti*, and the sun is located in the *nābhicakra*.
All [the senses] are bound by the *mudrā*, while the beautiful eye is fixed on the tip of the nose. (15)

The letter *a* is in the region of fire (the navel), the letter *u* is situated in the heart, and the letter *m* is between the eyebrows; one should understand this from the [following] statement. || 16 ||
The Brahma-knot is located below the navel, the Viṣṇu-knot resides in the heart, and the Rudra-knot is between the eyebrows; thus these three are released.
They say that the syllable *a* is Brahman; the syllable *u* is said to be Viṣṇu;
and in the syllable *m*, Śiva himself is present—the supreme, more peaceful than peace itself. (18)
Having constricted the throat, one should firmly restrain the two channels;
while the tongue is pressed [against the palate], sixteen [breaths] move upwards.
Trikūṭa, Trihaṭha, Golhāṭa, and likewise Śikhara;
Triśikha, Vajra, Oṃkāra, Mūrdhan, Ākha, Bhruva, and Mukha. || 20 ||
One should contract the sun (the right channel) itself, and thereafter the channel proceeds [to flow].
Upon their piercing, there occurs the union of the three-fold haṭha, and the vision of the moon from both [channels]. || 21 ||
Praṇavā, Gudanālā, Nalinī, Sarpiṇī, Baṅkanālī, Kṣayā, Śaurī, Kuṇḍalī, and Kundalā are recorded [as the names of the channels]. || 22 ||
One should move Kuṇḍalī; when the lunar orb is pierced by the vital breath (prāṇa), the Vajra-clusters are perfected, and one should bind the nine gates. || 23 ||
Mounted upon the purifying *sumana* tree, he was likewise deeply absorbed in the *nirguṇa* state;
by the resonance of the abode of Brahman, she [the river] became the showerer of nectar in the *śaṅkhinī*.
One should illuminate the lamp of knowledge, which is the extraction of the maṇḍala of the six cakras;
the bathing of all [deities] is performed within the body, and the worship of the deities is carried out. || 25 ||
Having bathed the Lord, whose nature is consciousness, with the nectar of the moon through devotion,
one should likewise offer the flower of the mind and worship the supreme Śiva.
Having beheld that stainless one whose nature is knowledge and who is free from all affliction, he is seen in the form of the body, though he is all-pervading and untainted. || 27 ||
The word "haṃsa, haṃsa" resides within the bodies of living beings;
it is said to be the knot formed by the union of the prāṇa and apāna breaths. || 28 ||
One thousand, one hundred and six [breaths] always pass from the seat of excretion; that is called "Haṃsa So'ham. || 29 ||
The Liṅga of the Fire (Agni) is in the eastern part, and that of Śaṅkhinī is in the western;
the Jyotirliṅga, which is Śiva consisting of red and white, is in the middle of the eyebrows.
In the eastern and western directions, situated upon the Vajradaṇḍa, the two locations of the sixty Bhoginīs reveal the Paśu-liṅga. || 31 ||
The supreme place, cool beyond cool and filled with fat and marrow,
flows from the abode of Brahmā and sprinkles the three worlds.
The ritual procedure for all diseases, involving the balance of wind and bile and free from the eighteen defects, is proclaimed by Mīnanātha. (33)
Thus ends the Bhaktisaṃ, composed by Matsyendranātha.
